claim: Eye movements provide insights about a wide range of brain functions, from sensorimotor integration to cognition.
source: Eye movements provide insights about a wide range of brain functions, from sensorimotor integration to cognition; hence, the measurement of eye movements is an important tool in neuroscience research.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of eye movements in neuroscience, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A small magnet was surgically implanted on the eye, and changes in the magnet angle as the eye rotated were detected by a magnetic field sensor.
source: A small magnet was surgically implanted on the eye, and changes in the magnet angle as the eye rotated were detected by a magnetic field sensor.
evidence: This describes the method developed in this study, which is supported by the experimental procedures and data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Systematic testing demonstrated high resolution measurements of eye position of <0.1°.
source: Systematic testing demonstrated high resolution measurements of eye position of <0.1°.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 5B.

claim: Magnetic eye tracking provides the first method for reliable, high-resolution measurement of eye movements in freely moving mice.
source: Most notably, it provides the first method for reliable, high-resolution measurement of eye movements in freely moving mice, revealing increased eye movements and altered binocular coordination compared to head-fixed mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing eye movements in freely moving mice (Figure 7) and by comparison with previous methods discussed in the introduction.

claim: Freely moving mice showed increased eye movements compared to head-fixed mice.
source: Most notably, it provides the first method for reliable, high-resolution measurement of eye movements in freely moving mice, revealing increased eye movements and altered binocular coordination compared to head-fixed mice.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7C and 7E.

claim: Freely moving mice showed altered binocular coordination compared to head-fixed mice.
source: Most notably, it provides the first method for reliable, high-resolution measurement of eye movements in freely moving mice, revealing increased eye movements and altered binocular coordination compared to head-fixed mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7G showing changes in eye divergence.

claim: Vision is actively controlled by eye movements, which localize and stabilize images on the retina.
source: Vision is actively controlled by eye movements, which localize and stabilize images on the retina.
evidence: This is established knowledge in vision science.

claim: The analysis of eye movements can provide a window on a variety of sensory, motor, and cognitive functions, such as attention, learning and memory, and decision-making.
source: The analysis of eye movements can provide a window on a variety of sensory, motor, and cognitive functions, such as attention, learning and memory, and decision-making (Duhamel et al., 1992; Kustov and Robinson, 1996; Raposo et al., 2012; Raymond and Lisberger, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Abnormal eye movements are associated with numerous cognitive disorders, including autism, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease.
source: Moreover, abnormal eye movements are associated with numerous cognitive disorders, including autism, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease (Avanzini et al., 1979; DeJong and Jones, 1971; Holzman et al., 1976; Rosenhall et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Measurements of eye movements have been routinely implemented in neuroscientific studies of primates.
source: Given their broad utility, measurements of eye movements have been routinely implemented in neuroscientific studies of primates.
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in the field, based on established knowledge.

claim: Measurements of eye movements are uncommon in mice.
source: In contrast, such measurements are uncommon in mice, a species that is widely used in molecular and genetic studies of behavior (Beery and Zucker, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by citation and general knowledge.

claim: Mice encode visual input with high selectivity.
source: Although less dependent on vision than primates, mice encode visual input with high selectivity (Niell and Stryker, 2008), and use vision for a variety of functions including navigation (Chapillon, 1999; Chen et al., 2013a; Hopkins, 1953; Saleem et al., 2013), avoidance of predators (Yilmaz and Meister, 2013), and recognition of territorial boundaries (Mackintosh, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Niell and Stryker, 2008.

claim: Mice use vision for navigation.
source: Although less dependent on vision than primates, mice encode visual input with high selectivity (Niell and Stryker, 2008), and use vision for a variety of functions including navigation (Chapillon, 1999; Chen et al., 2013a; Hopkins, 1953; Saleem et al., 2013), avoidance of predators (Yilmaz and Meister, 2013), and recognition of territorial boundaries (Mackintosh, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mice use vision for avoidance of predators.
source: Although less dependent on vision than primates, mice encode visual input with high selectivity (Niell and Stryker, 2008), and use vision for a variety of functions including navigation (Chapillon, 1999; Chen et al., 2013a; Hopkins, 1953; Saleem et al., 2013), avoidance of predators (Yilmaz and Meister, 2013), and recognition of territorial boundaries (Mackintosh, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yilmaz and Meister, 2013.

claim: Mice use vision for recognition of territorial boundaries.
source: Although less dependent on vision than primates, mice encode visual input with high selectivity (Niell and Stryker, 2008), and use vision for a variety of functions including navigation (Chapillon, 1999; Chen et al., 2013a; Hopkins, 1953; Saleem et al., 2013), avoidance of predators (Yilmaz and Meister, 2013), and recognition of territorial boundaries (Mackintosh, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mackintosh, 1973.

claim: The main obstacle to measuring eye movements in mice is their diminutive size.
source: The main obstacle to measuring eye movements in mice is their diminutive size.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical challenges in the field, based on knowledge and inference.

claim: Average eye diameter is only 3.4 mm in mice.
source: In particular, the small eye restricts what can be implanted on the eye's surface: average eye diameter is only 3.4 mm in mice (Remtulla and Hallett, 1985), compared to 6.4 mm in rat (Chaudhuri et al., 1983), 9.2 mm in chicken (Schwarz et al., 2013), 18 mm in rabbit (Hughes, 1972), and 21 mm in rhesus macaque (Schultz, 1940).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Remtulla and Hallett, 1985.

claim: Average eye diameter is 6.4 mm in rat.
source: In particular, the small eye restricts what can be implanted on the eye's surface: average eye diameter is only 3.4 mm in mice (Remtulla and Hallett, 1985), compared to 6.4 mm in rat (Chaudhuri et al., 1983), 9.2 mm in chicken (Schwarz et al., 2013), 18 mm in rabbit (Hughes, 1972), and 21 mm in rhesus macaque (Schultz, 1940).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chaudhuri et al., 1983.

claim: Average eye diameter is 9.2 mm in chicken.
source: In particular, the small eye restricts what can be implanted on the eye's surface: average eye diameter is only 3.4 mm in mice (Remtulla and Hallett, 1985), compared to 6.4 mm in rat (Chaudhuri et al., 1983), 9.2 mm in chicken (Schwarz et al., 2013), 18 mm in rabbit (Hughes, 1972), and 21 mm in rhesus macaque (Schultz, 1940).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schwarz et al., 2013.

claim: Average eye diameter is 18 mm in rabbit.
source: In particular, the small eye restricts what can be implanted on the eye's surface: average eye diameter is only 3.4 mm in mice (Remtulla and Hallett, 1985), compared to 6.4 mm in rat (Chaudhuri et al., 1983), 9.2 mm in chicken (Schwarz et al., 2013), 18 mm in rabbit (Hughes, 1972), and 21 mm in rhesus macaque (Schultz, 1940).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hughes, 1972.

claim: Average eye diameter is 21 mm in rhesus macaque.
source: In particular, the small eye restricts what can be implanted on the eye's surface: average eye diameter is only 3.4 mm in mice (Remtulla and Hallett, 1985), compared to 6.4 mm in rat (Chaudhuri et al., 1983), 9.2 mm in chicken (Schwarz et al., 2013), 18 mm in rabbit (Hughes, 1972), and 21 mm in rhesus macaque (Schultz, 1940).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schultz, 1940.

claim: The only eye tracking method compatible with free motion in small animals was the electro-oculogram, which is susceptible to inaccuracies.
source: Previously, the only eye tracking method compatible with free motion in small animals was the electro-oculogram, which is susceptible to inaccuracies (Arden and Kelsey, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arden and Kelsey, 1962.

claim: Video-oculography was used to measure visually driven eye movements in mice without head restraint, however the mice were constrained to a small platform, and only 20% of the measurements were useable.
source: Recently, video-oculography was used to measure visually driven eye movements in mice without head restraint, however the mice were constrained to a small platform, and only 20% of the measurements were useable (Kretschmer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kretschmer et al., 2017.

claim: The eye coil technique is considered the gold standard for measuring eye movements in most species.
source: The eye coil, or scleral search coil, technique is considered the gold standard for measuring eye movements in most species (Boyden and Raymond, 2003; Collewijn et al., 1975; Judge et al., 1980; Koekkoek et al., 1997; Remmel, 1984; Robinson, 1963).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The eye coil method has high spatial resolution of ~0.1°.
source: A major advantage of the eye coil method is that it has high spatial (~0.1°) and temporal (<1 ms) resolution (Collewijn et al., 1975; Stahl et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Collewijn et al., 1975 and Stahl et al., 2000.

claim: The eye coil method has high temporal resolution of <1 ms.
source: A major advantage of the eye coil method is that it has high spatial (~0.1°) and temporal (<1 ms) resolution (Collewijn et al., 1975; Stahl et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Collewijn et al., 1975 and Stahl et al., 2000.

claim: The spatial resolution of video-oculography is lower than that of the eye coil.
source: Its spatial resolution is lower than that of the eye coil (Houben et al., 2006; Kimmel et al., 2012; McCamy et al., 2015; Stahl et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Inaccuracies in video-oculography can arise from changes in pupil diameter due to fluctuations in luminance or behavioral state.
source: Inaccuracies can arise from changes in pupil diameter due to fluctuations in luminance or behavioral state (Kaufman, 2002; Kimmel et al., 2012; McCamy et al., 2015; Reimer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Three previous reports, two in goldfish and one in chickens, have demonstrated the potential of magnetic sensing for measuring eye movements.
source: Three previous reports, two in goldfish (Rodríguez et al., 2001; Salas et al., 1999) and one in chickens (Schwarz et al., 2013) have demonstrated the potential of magnetic sensing for measuring eye movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A 0.75 × 2 mm cylinder magnet was positioned directly below and adjacent to the sensor, with the N-S axis of the magnet parallel to the plane of the sensor.
source: Initially, a 0.75 × 2 mm cylinder magnet was positioned directly below and adjacent to the sensor, with the N-S axis of the magnet parallel to the plane of the sensor, and the magnet's axis of rotation aligned to the center of the sensor (Figure 1A, left, with δ = 0 mm).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup, supported by Figure 1A.

claim: When the magnet was rotated ±90° about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the sensor, the magnetic sensor produced a voltage that depended on the angle of the magnet.
source: When the magnet was rotated ±90° about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the sensor, the magnetic sensor produced a voltage that depended on the angle of the magnet (Figure 1A, center, black traces).
evidence: This describes experimental results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The magnetic sensor has two channels, which relay output from two sets of magnetoresistive elements at a 45° orientation relative to each other.
source: The magnetic sensor we used has two channels, which relay output from two sets of magnetoresistive elements at a 45° orientation relative to each other, so that the position tuning of the two channels is offset by 45° (Figure 1A, center).
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the sensor, supported by Figure 1A.

claim: Sensitivity decreased from 224.7 ± 0.3 mV/° at 0 mm to 28.1 ± 1.0 mV/° at 5 mm.
source: Sensitivity decreased from 224.7 ± 0.3 mV/° at 0 mm to 28.1 ± 1.0 mV/° at 5 mm (average sensitivity of the two channels; sensitivity for each channel is shown separately in Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At 3 mm, the sensitivity was 127.0 ± 1.2 mV/°.
source: Notably, at 3 mm, a distance readily achievable in mice (see Materials and methods), the sensitivity was 127.0 ± 1.2 mV/°.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments.

claim: At 3 mm distance, the spatial resolution was 0.016° ± 0.005°.
source: This corresponded to a spatial resolution, as measured by the standard deviation of the signal at rest, of 0.016° ± 0.005°, which is nearly an order of magnitude below the noise floor measured by the best eye tracking methods in mice (Stahl et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments, with comparison to previous work via citation.

claim: Tilting the magnet by 45° did not affect sensitivity.
source: Tilting the magnet by 45° did not affect sensitivity (127.8 ± 4 mV/° no tilt, 128.0 ± 2.0 mV/° with 45° tilt, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A cylinder magnet was surgically implanted beneath the conjunctiva on the temporal margin of one eye, with the N-S axis aligned so that it created a rotating magnetic field during horizontal (nasal-temporal) eye movements.
source: A cylinder magnet was surgically implanted beneath the conjunctiva on the temporal margin of one eye, with the N-S axis aligned so that it created a rotating magnetic field during horizontal (nasal-temporal) eye movements (Figure 2A; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure used in the study, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) drives compensatory eye movements in response to passive head rotation in the dark, in mice.
source: The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) drives compensatory eye movements in response to passive head rotation in the dark, in mice (Iwashita et al., 2001; Katoh et al., 1998; Kimpo et al., 2005; van Alphen et al., 2001) as in other species.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: When vestibular stimuli were delivered to mice implanted with the magnetic eye tracking system, the magnetic sensor detected robust eye movements driven by the VOR.
source: Accordingly, when vestibular stimuli were delivered to mice implanted with the magnetic eye tracking system, the magnetic sensor detected robust eye movements driven by the VOR.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sinusoidal vestibular stimuli at a range of stimulus frequencies from 0.2 Hz to 5 Hz elicited sinusoidal eye movements at the corresponding frequencies.
source: Sinusoidal vestibular stimuli at a range of stimulus frequencies from 0.2 Hz to 5 Hz elicited sinusoidal eye movements at the corresponding frequencies (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The optokinetic reflex (OKR) drives image-stabilizing eye movements in response to motion of a visual stimulus, in mice.
source: The optokinetic reflex (OKR) drives image-stabilizing eye movements in response to motion of a visual stimulus, in mice (Iwashita et al., 2001; Katoh et al., 1998) as in other species.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: When a striped drum was rotated around the mouse, the magnetic sensor detected robust eye movements driven by the OKR, at all stimulus frequencies tested (0.2 Hz–5 Hz).
source: Accordingly, when a striped drum was rotated around the mouse, the magnetic sensor detected robust eye movements driven by the OKR, at all stimulus frequencies tested (0.2 Hz–5 Hz; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In species other than primates, eye position is typically computed from video measurements using an estimate of Rp, the distance of the pupil from the center of corneal curvature.
source: In species other than primates, eye position is typically computed from video measurements using an estimate of Rp, the distance of the pupil from the center of corneal curvature (Figure 3A; Stahl et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes standard practice in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Difficulty in estimating Rp and variations in Rp across individuals and during the course of an experiment are sources of inaccuracy in video-oculography.
source: However, difficulty in estimating Rp and variations in Rp across individuals and during the course of an experiment are sources of inaccuracy (Kaufman, 2002; Kimmel et al., 2012; McCamy et al., 2015; Reimer et al., 2014; Wisard et al., 2010; Zoccolan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The dual-angle video-oculography system eliminates the need to estimate Rp by using simultaneous image capture of the eye from two cameras.
source: We eliminated the need to estimate Rp by using simultaneous image capture of the eye from two cameras.
evidence: This describes the methodological innovation developed in this study.

claim: The eye position measured with dual-angle video-oculography agreed closely with true position over the full range of ± 25°.
source: To validate the dual-angle video-oculography system, two mice were anesthetized and the cameras were rotated at known angles around one eye, over a ± 25° range. The eye position measured with video-oculography agreed closely with true position over the full range (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the validation experiment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Incorporating both channels of the magnetic sensor only improved the fit to the video-derived measurements by a small amount (3.5% additional variance explained).
source: On average, incorporating both channels only improved the fit to the video-derived measurements by a small amount (3.5% additional variance explained, Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis, shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Including a nonlinear, quadratic term for each channel provided little additional improvement (2.3% additional variance explained compared to the two-channel model).
source: We also estimated eye position using a model that included a nonlinear, quadratic term for each channel, and found little additional improvement (2.3% additional variance explained compared to the two-channel model, Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis, shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The sensitivity of the magnetic sensor decreased by only 4.2% after one week.
source: On average, the sensitivity of the magnetic sensor decreased by only 4.2% after one week (Figure 4E, left).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from longitudinal measurements, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In a population of ten mice recorded 5–7 months after implantation, only two had unusable eye movement signals.
source: Even after many months, the magnetic implants were remarkably robust. In a population of ten mice recorded 5–7 months after implantation, only two had unusable eye movement signals.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from long-term follow-up measurements.

claim: The correlation coefficient for the magnetic system was comparable to that for the eye coil system.
source: Both eye coil and magnetic systems were highly correlated with the video system, and the correlation coefficient for the magnetic system was comparable to that for the eye coil system (Figure 5A), indicating a similar level of linearity.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The magnetic and eye coil systems each had spatial resolutions of <0.1°.
source: Quantified in this way, the magnetic and eye coil systems each had spatial resolutions of <0.1° (Figure 5B), similar to previous reports for the eye coil (Stahl et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparison, shown in Figure 5B, with reference to previous work.

claim: Neither the gain nor the phase of the eye movement responses were altered after magnet implantation.
source: Neither the gain nor the phase of the eye movement responses were altered after magnet implantation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 6.

claim: The gain and phase of the VOR measured with magnetic eye tracking were in the range reported previously in mice.
source: The gain and phase of the VOR measured with magnetic eye tracking (Figure 6, dashed, blue lines) were in the range reported previously in mice by our laboratory (Kimpo and Raymond, 2007) and other laboratories (Iwashita et al., 2001; van Alphen et al., 2001), as were the gain and phase of the visually driven eye movements elicited by an optokinetic stimulus at a range of frequencies (Figure 6—figure supplement 2; Iwashita et al., 2001; Kimpo and Raymond, 2007; Tabata et al., 2010; van Alphen et al., 2001, 2009, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous studies via citations and data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The amplitude of the signal in the sensor contralateral to the eye with the magnet was only 2.7 ± 0.9% of that in the ipsilateral sensor, indicating limited crosstalk.
source: The amplitude of the signal in the sensor contralateral to the eye with the magnet was only 2.7 ± 0.9% of that in the ipsilateral sensor, indicating limited crosstalk.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments testing bilateral recording.

claim: Freely moving mice displayed a two-fold increase in the standard deviation of eye position compared to head-fixed mice.
source: On average, freely moving mice displayed a two-fold increase in the standard deviation of eye position (Figure 7C), as well as a four-fold increase in the mean speed of the eye (Figure 7E) compared to head-fixed mice.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the freely moving experiments, shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Freely moving mice displayed a four-fold increase in the mean speed of the eye compared to head-fixed mice.
source: On average, freely moving mice displayed a two-fold increase in the standard deviation of eye position (Figure 7C), as well as a four-fold increase in the mean speed of the eye (Figure 7E) compared to head-fixed mice.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the freely moving experiments, shown in Figure 7E.

claim: During active, self-generated body movements, the mean eye speed was higher compared to when the body was relatively still.
source: During active, self-generated body movements, the mean eye speed was higher compared to when the body was relatively still (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: There was a strong, linear relationship between self-generated head movements about the yaw axis and horizontal eye movements in the opposite direction.
source: There was a strong, linear relationship between self-generated head movements about the yaw axis and horizontal eye movements in the opposite direction (Figure 7F), suggesting that active head movements are a major driver of eye movements in freely moving mice.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The eye divergence increased in unrestrained mice, compared to during head fixation.
source: We found that the eye divergence (the horizontal angular distance between the two eyes) increased in unrestrained mice, compared to during head fixation (Figure 7G, left), and the variability of eye divergence also increased (Figure 7G, right).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The variability of eye divergence increased in unrestrained mice compared to during head fixation.
source: We found that the eye divergence (the horizontal angular distance between the two eyes) increased in unrestrained mice, compared to during head fixation (Figure 7G, left), and the variability of eye divergence also increased (Figure 7G, right).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Magnetic eye tracking provides a high-resolution (<0.1°) method for measuring eye movements that overcomes the challenging physical constraints of small and freely moving animals.
source: Magnetic eye tracking opens up exciting new scientific opportunities by providing a high-resolution (<0.1°) method for measuring eye movements that overcomes the challenging physical constraints of small and freely moving animals.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The spatial resolution of magnetic eye tracking (0.098°) was comparable to the resolution of the eye coil technique in mice, as measured by our lab (0.091°) and other labs (0.09°).
source: The spatial resolution of magnetic eye tracking (0.098°) was comparable to the resolution of the eye coil technique in mice, as measured by our lab (0.091°; Figure 5B) and other labs (0.09°, Stahl et al., 2000), and was also comparable to the resolution of the eye coil technique in larger species such as monkeys (<0.1°, Kimmel et al., 2012) and humans (0.096°, Houben et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 5B and citations to previous work.

claim: The spatial resolution of magnetic eye tracking was comparable to the resolution of the eye coil technique in monkeys (<0.1°).
source: The spatial resolution of magnetic eye tracking (0.098°) was comparable to the resolution of the eye coil technique in mice, as measured by our lab (0.091°; Figure 5B) and other labs (0.09°, Stahl et al., 2000), and was also comparable to the resolution of the eye coil technique in larger species such as monkeys (<0.1°, Kimmel et al., 2012) and humans (0.096°, Houben et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kimmel et al., 2012.

claim: The spatial resolution of magnetic eye tracking was comparable to the resolution of the eye coil technique in humans (0.096°).
source: The spatial resolution of magnetic eye tracking (0.098°) was comparable to the resolution of the eye coil technique in mice, as measured by our lab (0.091°; Figure 5B) and other labs (0.09°, Stahl et al., 2000), and was also comparable to the resolution of the eye coil technique in larger species such as monkeys (<0.1°, Kimmel et al., 2012) and humans (0.096°, Houben et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Houben et al., 2006.

claim: The performance of the magnetic eye tracking system benefited from the use of angular magnetic field sensors containing anisotropic magnetoresistive (AMR) technology.
source: The performance of the magnetic eye tracking system benefited from the use of angular magnetic field sensors containing anisotropic magnetoresistive (AMR) technology (Schwarz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the technology used, supported by citation.

claim: AMR sensors can achieve high resolution, while satisfying the constraints of low power, low cost, and small sensor size.
source: AMR sensors can achieve high resolution, while satisfying the constraints of low power, low cost, and small sensor size (Lenz and Edelstein, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lenz and Edelstein, 2006.

claim: Magnetic eye tracking is far less expensive than commercially available eye coil systems.
source: Magnetic eye tracking is also far less expensive than commercially available eye coil systems, making this approach available to more investigators.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on knowledge of the costs of the two systems.

claim: The lack of fragile wires in magnetic eye tracking minimizes the difficulty of surgical implantation, greatly reducing the time required for the experimenter to learn and perform the procedure.
source: A third key advantage of magnetic eye tracking is the lack of fragile wires leading to the eye, which minimizes the difficulty of surgical implantation, greatly reducing the time required for the experimenter to learn and perform the procedure.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the authors' experience with both methods.

claim: The wires used for eye coil recordings often fail after several weeks following implantation.
source: The lack of fragile wires also extends the long-term reliability of the magnet implants. Only two out of ten mice followed for half a year after surgery had failed magnet implants, whereas the wires used for eye coil recordings often fail after several weeks following implantation (Stahl et al., 2000; Raymond lab, unpublished observations).
evidence: This is supported by citation and unpublished observations.

claim: The spatial resolution of video-oculography in rodents is 0.23° or ~1°.
source: First, the spatial resolution of magnetic eye tracking (0.1°) is superior to what has been reported for video-oculography in rodents (0.23°, Stahl et al., 2000; ~1°, Wallace et al., 2013), in monkeys (video resolution 2‒3 × worse than eye coil, Kimmel et al. (2012); McCamy et al., 2015) and in humans (0.56°, Houben et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In monkeys, video-oculography resolution is 2‒3 × worse than eye coil.
source: First, the spatial resolution of magnetic eye tracking (0.1°) is superior to what has been reported for video-oculography in rodents (0.23°, Stahl et al., 2000; ~1°, Wallace et al., 2013), in monkeys (video resolution 2‒3 × worse than eye coil, Kimmel et al. (2012); McCamy et al., 2015) and in humans (0.56°, Houben et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kimmel et al., 2012 and McCamy et al., 2015.

claim: In humans, video-oculography resolution is 0.56°.
source: First, the spatial resolution of magnetic eye tracking (0.1°) is superior to what has been reported for video-oculography in rodents (0.23°, Stahl et al., 2000; ~1°, Wallace et al., 2013), in monkeys (video resolution 2‒3 × worse than eye coil, Kimmel et al. (2012); McCamy et al., 2015) and in humans (0.56°, Houben et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Houben et al., 2006.

claim: The hardware required for magnetic eye tracking is more than an order of magnitude lighter (0.05 cm3 and 0.180 g total) than video-oculography systems for rats.
source: Technological advances have reduced the size of cameras to fit on the head of a rat (Wallace et al., 2013), but the hardware required for magnetic eye tracking is more than an order of magnitude lighter (0.05 cm3 and 0.180 g total) and is therefore trivial for a mouse to carry, allowing much greater mobility than possible with video-oculography (Kretschmer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison based on the specifications of the magnetic eye tracking system and citations to previous work.

claim: Gaze direction may deviate substantially from head direction in freely moving mice.
source: Our finding of robust eye movements in freely moving mice (Figure 7) suggests that gaze direction deviates substantially from head direction, as previously reported in rats (Wallace et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 7 and supported by citation to Wallace et al., 2013.

claim: Magnetic eye tracking and video-oculography were performed in 35 C57BL/6 mice and two hybrid C57BL/6 × 129S1/SvImJ F2 mice.
source: Magnetic eye tracking and video-oculography were performed in 35 C57BL/6 mice and two hybrid C57BL/6 × 129S1/SvImJ F2 mice.
evidence: This describes the sample used in the study.

claim: Eye coil and video-oculography recordings were made in an additional nine C57BL/6 mice.
source: Eye coil and video-oculography recordings were made in an additional nine C57BL/6 mice.
evidence: This describes the sample used for the eye coil comparison.

claim: Most mice were implanted with two neodymium magnets of size 0.75 × 1 mm (diameter × height, grade N50, axially magnetized), which were stacked end-to-end for a total size of 0.75 × 2 mm (weight: 6.8 mg).
source: Most mice were implanted with two neodymium magnets of size 0.75 × 1 mm (diameter × height, grade N50, axially magnetized, SuperMagnetMan.com), which were stacked end-to-end for a total size of 0.75 × 2 mm (weight: 6.8 mg).
evidence: This describes the materials and methods used in the study.

claim: Cylinder magnets were implanted in a single eye in 24 mice, and bilaterally in an additional seven mice.
source: Cylinder magnets were implanted in a single eye in 24 mice, and bilaterally in an additional seven mice.
evidence: This describes the sample and procedures used in the study.

claim: The sensor was positioned as close as possible to the eye (2.7 ± 0.2 mm, n = 8 mice, distance from the bottom surface of the sensor to the nasal-temporal axis defined by the two corners of the eye).
